hero.basedOn: A BMJ analysis article pooled two meta-analyses: 281 studies from 36 countries where people filled in the Yale Food Addiction Scale questionnaire. 14% of adults (12% of children) scored at the 'food addiction' level.
hero.caveat: A questionnaire score, not a diagnosis, and most samples were not national. Another pooling of 272 studies, which included clinic patients, found 20%.
hero.numberCheck: 14% matches the BMJ text (re-fetched). Praxedes 2022 (PMID 34953001, abstract fetched) gives 20% across 272 studies, higher in clinical samples and 55% in people with binge eating; the caveat names the 20%.

ref.cite: Gearhardt AN, Bueno NB, DiFeliceantonio AG, Roberto CA, Jimenez-Murcia S, Fernandez-Aranda F (2023). Social, clinical, and policy implications of ultra-processed food addiction. BMJ 383:e075354.
ref.quote: A recent analysis of two systematic reviews including 281 studies from 36 different countries found the overall pooled prevalence of food addiction using YFAS was 14% in adults

stats.line: US adults aged 19 to 39 get about 54% of their daily calories from ultra-processed food.
stats.mirror: You get half your food from packets, boxes and drive-throughs.

basis.design: national survey (NHANES), one day's diet recall interview
basis.who: US adults aged 19 to 39, men and women
basis.measured: Share of calories from ultra-processed food (NOVA groups). Men of all ages: 53.3% (2,146 men). Biggest sources for adults: sandwiches and burgers, sweet bakery products, then sugary drinks.

stats.caveat: This is what most people eat; it is not a sign of addiction. One day's recall can miss or misreport foods.

ref.cite: Williams AM, Couch CA, Emmerich SD, Ogburn DF (2025). Ultra-processed food consumption in youth and adults: United States, August 2021-August 2023. NCHS Data Brief No. 536.
ref.quote: Adults ages 19–39 consumed 54.4% of calories from ultra-processed foods.

stats.line: In 23 US states, 43% of adults aged 18 to 24 had a sugary drink at least once a day, more than any other age group.
stats.mirror: You drink soda, sweet tea or energy drinks every single day.

basis.design: state phone surveys (Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System)
basis.who: US adults in 23 states and Washington DC; this figure is 18- to 24-year-olds, men and women
basis.n: 157,668 adults answered (the report didn't say how many were aged 18 to 24)
basis.measured: Drinking regular soda, fruit drinks, sweet tea, or sports or energy drinks at least once a day. Diet drinks and 100% juice did not count. Men of all ages: 34.1%.

stats.caveat: Self-reported by phone, and older data. Answers given per week or month were turned into a daily figure.

ref.cite: Park S, Xu F, Town M, Blanck HM (2016). Prevalence of sugar-sweetened beverage intake among adults — 23 states and the District of Columbia, 2013. MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report 65(7):169-174.
ref.quote: At least once daily SSB intake was most common among persons aged 18–24 years (43.3%), men (34.1%),

stats.line: About 2 in 100 US men have had binge-eating disorder at some point; counting milder binge eating, 4 in 100.
stats.mirror: You eat until it hurts, then hide the wrappers.

basis.design: national survey, face-to-face interviews (National Comorbidity Survey Replication)
basis.who: US adults living in households; this figure is the men
basis.measured: Lifetime binge-eating disorder by a structured interview (DSM-IV rules). Any binge eating, milder cases included: 4.0% of men. Of everyone with the disorder, 43.6% ever sought treatment for it.

stats.caveat: Old data and older diagnostic rules. Lifetime means 'ever', so it includes men who have since recovered.

ref.cite: Hudson JI, Hiripi E, Pope HG, Kessler RC (2007). The prevalence and correlates of eating disorders in the National Comorbidity Survey Replication. Biological Psychiatry 61(3):348-358.
ref.quote: Lifetime prevalence estimates of DSM-IV anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, and binge eating disorder are .9%, 1.5%, and 3.5% among women, and .3% .5%, and 2.0% among men.

stats.line: Across 14 countries, only 38% of people who had binge-eating disorder ever got treatment for it.
stats.mirror: You have never told anyone about the binges.

basis.design: cross-national surveys, face-to-face interviews (WHO World Mental Health)
basis.who: adults aged 18+, men and women, who had ever had binge-eating disorder
basis.where: 14 countries: Colombia, Brazil (Sao Paulo), Mexico, Romania, Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, New Zealand, Northern Ireland, Portugal, Spain, USA
basis.measured: Ever getting treatment specifically for eating problems. 57.7% got treatment for some emotional problem.

stats.caveat: Mostly richer countries. Treatment is self-reported and recalled. Women were more likely than men to get treatment.

ref.cite: Kessler RC, Berglund PA, Chiu WT, et al. (2013). The prevalence and correlates of binge eating disorder in the World Health Organization World Mental Health Surveys. Biological Psychiatry 73(9):904-914.
ref.quote: Smaller proportions of lifetime cases (BN 47.4%, BED 38.3%) ever received treatment specifically for eating disorders

stats.line: By 2018, US kids and teens got 67% of their calories from ultra-processed food, up from 61% in 1999.
stats.mirror: You grew up on cereal, chips and soda, like most kids did.

basis.design: national survey, 10 rounds (NHANES), one day's diet recall
basis.who: US children and teens aged 2 to 19; about half boys
basis.measured: Share of calories from ultra-processed food (NOVA groups). Sweet snacks and sweets rose from 10.7% to 12.9% of calories; sugary drinks fell from 10.8% to 5.3%.

stats.caveat: One day of eating per child, recalled in an interview. Shows what kids ate, not that it caused habits later.

ref.cite: Wang L, Martínez Steele E, Du M, Pomeranz JL, O'Connor LE, Herrick KA, Luo H, Zhang X, Mozaffarian D, Zhang FF (2021). Trends in consumption of ultraprocessed foods among US youths aged 2-19 years, 1999-2018. JAMA 326(6):519-530.
ref.quote: From 1999 to 2018, the estimated percentage of total energy from consumption of ultraprocessed foods increased from 61.4% to 67.0%

stats.line: Cravings and food cues explain about 11% of later eating and weight gain; food pictures and videos pull as hard as real food.
stats.mirror: You get hungry watching food videos late at night.

basis.design: meta-analysis of 45 reports (69 results)
basis.who: children and adults, lean and heavy
basis.measured: Link between reacting to food cues or craving, and later eating or weight gain (r = 0.33, medium). Same size across body weight, age and dieting.

stats.caveat: A link, not proof that cues cause weight gain. 11% means most of what you eat is explained by other things.

ref.cite: Boswell RG, Kober H (2016). Food cue reactivity and craving predict eating and weight gain: a meta-analytic review. Obesity Reviews 17(2):159-177.
ref.quote: we found an overall medium effect of food cue reactivity and craving on outcomes (r = 0.33, p < 0.001; approximately 11% of variance)

stats.line: Binge-eating disorder usually starts in the late teens or early 20s; the middle age of onset was about 19.
stats.mirror: You started bingeing around college or your first job.

basis.design: cross-national surveys, face-to-face interviews (WHO World Mental Health)
basis.who: adults aged 18+, men and women, who had ever had binge-eating disorder
basis.where: 14 countries: Colombia, Brazil (Sao Paulo), Mexico, Romania, Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, New Zealand, Northern Ireland, Portugal, Spain, USA
basis.measured: Age when symptoms first started, recalled in an interview. Median 19.3 years for binge-eating disorder (18.0 for bulimia).

stats.caveat: Age is remembered, often years later. In the US survey, eating problems started at a median age of 18 to 21.

ref.cite: Kessler RC, Berglund PA, Chiu WT, et al. (2013). The prevalence and correlates of binge eating disorder in the World Health Organization World Mental Health Surveys. Biological Psychiatry 73(9):904-914.
ref.quote: Both mean and median AOO are consistently earlier for BN than BED (means: 20.6 vs. 23.3, t=3.4, p<.001; medians: 18.0 vs. 19.3).

stats.line: On ultra-processed food, people ate about 500 more calories a day and gained about 0.9 kg in two weeks.
stats.mirror: You eat until you're full, yet still take in far too much.

basis.design: randomised crossover trial (inpatient)
basis.who: weight-stable adults, mean age 31, average BMI 27
basis.measured: Food eaten when free to eat as much as wanted, weighed by staff. Meals matched for calories offered, sugar, fat, fibre and salt.

stats.caveat: Only 20 people, in hospital, for two weeks. They also ate faster on ultra-processed food (17 kcal a minute more).

ref.cite: Hall KD, Ayuketah A, Brychta R, et al. (2019). Ultra-processed diets cause excess calorie intake and weight gain: an inpatient randomized controlled trial of ad libitum food intake. Cell Metabolism 30(1):67-77.
ref.quote: Energy intake was greater during the ultra-processed diet (508 ± 106 kcal/day; p = 0.0001)

stats.line: Over about 9 years, adults who ate the most ultra-processed food had a 26% higher risk of becoming overweight than those who ate the least.
stats.mirror: You eat packaged food most days and the weight creeps on.

basis.design: cohort followed for a median of 8.9 years (SUN study)
basis.who: middle-aged Spanish university graduates, not overweight at the start
basis.measured: Food eaten, from a 136-item food questionnaire, and new overweight or obesity. Top quarter of ultra-processed food eaters vs bottom quarter, allowing for other factors (hazard ratio 1.26).

stats.caveat: A link, not proof: people who eat more junk may differ in other ways. Food was self-reported. Graduates only.

ref.cite: Mendonça RD, Pimenta AM, Gea A, de la Fuente-Arrillaga C, Martinez-Gonzalez MA, Lopes AC, Bes-Rastrollo M (2016). Ultraprocessed food consumption and risk of overweight and obesity: the University of Navarra Follow-Up (SUN) cohort study. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition 104(5):1433-1440.
ref.quote: participants in the highest quartile of ultraprocessed food consumption were at a higher risk of developing overweight or obesity (adjusted HR: 1.26; 95% CI: 1.10, 1.45

stats.line: Binge-eating disorder typically lasts about 4 years; for the middle half of people, between 1 and 12 years.
stats.mirror: You have been 'starting Monday' for years.

basis.design: cross-national surveys, face-to-face interviews (WHO World Mental Health)
basis.who: adults aged 18+, men and women, who had ever had binge-eating disorder
basis.where: 14 countries: Colombia, Brazil (Sao Paulo), Mexico, Romania, Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, New Zealand, Northern Ireland, Portugal, Spain, USA
basis.measured: Years with the disorder, from recalled start to recovery or interview. Median 4.3 years; middle half of people 1.0 to 11.7 years.

stats.caveat: Recalled, and mixes treated and untreated people. People who started young tended to recover faster.

ref.cite: Kessler RC, Berglund PA, Chiu WT, et al. (2013). The prevalence and correlates of binge eating disorder in the World Health Organization World Mental Health Surveys. Biological Psychiatry 73(9):904-914.
ref.quote: Persistence is slightly higher for BN (6.5 years; 2.2–15.4) than BED (4.3 years; 1.0–11.7).

stats.line: People who cut down on junk food remember days 2 to 5 as the hardest.
stats.mirror: You cut out junk food and feel rough by day three.

basis.design: online survey (questionnaire development)
basis.who: adults aged 19-68 who had cut down on highly processed food in the past year; 51.9% women
basis.where: USA (online survey of paid task workers)
basis.measured: Recalled 'withdrawal' symptoms (mood, cravings, body) during a past attempt to cut down, on a new scale.

stats.caveat: Memory of a past attempt, online volunteers. A later trial (107 people) found cutting junk caused no more withdrawal than a normal diet.

ref.cite: Schulte EM, Smeal JK, Lewis J, Gearhardt AN (2018). Development of the Highly Processed Food Withdrawal Scale. Appetite 131:148-154.
ref.quote: symptoms assessed by the ProWS were reported as most intense between days 2-5 during an attempt to cut down

stats.line: In a trial of 107 dieters, cutting ultra-processed food caused no more withdrawal than a normal calorie-cut diet.
stats.mirror: You fear cutting junk food will feel like coming off a drug.

basis.design: secondary analysis of a randomised trial
basis.who: adults with obesity on a weight-loss diet
basis.n: 107 adults (51 normal diet, 56 diet plus cutting ultra-processed food)
basis.measured: Withdrawal scale scores on days 1, 3, 5 and 15. Difference 4.34 points, not statistically significant.

stats.caveat: Small, all dieting, only 16% had 'food addiction'. A small extra effect can't be ruled out. Anxious people reported more withdrawal in both groups.

ref.cite: Lopes NGDS, Ferreira CS, Silva-Junior AE, et al. (2026). Impact of dietary ultra-processed food restriction on withdrawal symptoms in individuals with obesity undergoing a weight loss diet. Clinical Nutrition ESPEN 76:105105.
ref.quote: A total of 107 participants were randomized (51 to ER-G and 56 to ER-UPF).

stats.line: In a trial of three treatments for binge eating, 7 in 10 people cut their binges by at least 70% within the first 4 weeks.
stats.mirror: You're starting treatment and wonder how soon the binges ease.

basis.design: randomised trial (interpersonal therapy, CBT guided self-help, or weight-loss treatment)
basis.who: adults with binge-eating disorder and overweight (BMI 27 to 45)
basis.n: 205 adults (145 cut their binges this fast)
basis.where: USA (Rutgers University, New Jersey, and Washington University, St. Louis)
basis.measured: A cut of 70% or more in binge eating by week 4 of treatment, and staying binge-free over the next 2 years.

stats.caveat: In guided self-help, fast starters stayed binge-free more often over 2 years. In interpersonal therapy, slow starters did just as well, so a slow start is not failure.

ref.cite: Hilbert A, Hildebrandt T, Agras WS, Wilfley DE, Wilson GT (2015). Rapid response in psychological treatments for binge eating disorder. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 83(3):649-654.
ref.quote: Defining rapid response as a reduction in binge-eating ≥ 70% by the fourth week of treatment, rapid response was identified in 70.7% of study participants (145/205).

stats.line: Slips are common: between one and four years after group CBT, 6 of 25 people slid back into binge eating.
stats.mirror: You binged again after a good run and think you failed.

basis.design: 4-year follow-up of a randomised trial
basis.who: adults with binge-eating disorder and overweight, about 80% women
basis.n: 25 people in the CBT group (of 90 in the trial)
basis.measured: Relapse to binge eating between the 1-year and 4-year checks, after 20 weekly group sessions of CBT. With interpersonal therapy: 3 of 30 (10%).

stats.caveat: One trial, mostly women. Even so, most were binge-free at 4 years.

ref.cite: Hilbert A, Bishop ME, Stein RI, et al. (2012). Long-term efficacy of psychological treatments for binge eating disorder. British Journal of Psychiatry 200(3):232-237.
ref.quote: 6 (24.0%) patients in the CBT and 3 (10.0%) in the IPT group relapsed

stats.line: On unprocessed food, the same people ate less without trying and lost about 0.9 kg in two weeks.
stats.mirror: You think losing weight means fighting hunger all day.

basis.design: randomised crossover trial (inpatient)
basis.who: weight-stable adults, mean age 31, average BMI 27
basis.measured: Body weight on each diet, free to eat as much as wanted. On unprocessed food the fullness hormone PYY rose and hunger hormone ghrelin fell.

stats.caveat: In hospital with meals cooked for them; 20 people; two weeks. Real life with shops and stress is harder.

ref.cite: Hall KD, Ayuketah A, Brychta R, et al. (2019). Ultra-processed diets cause excess calorie intake and weight gain: an inpatient randomized controlled trial of ad libitum food intake. Cell Metabolism 30(1):67-77.
ref.quote: participants gaining 0.9 ± 0.3 kg (p = 0.009) during the ultra-processed diet and losing 0.9 ± 0.3 kg (p = 0.007) during the unprocessed diet

stats.line: Eight weeks of home-cooked, minimally processed food brought about twice the weight loss of a 'healthy' packaged-food diet: 2.1% vs 1.1%.
stats.mirror: You eat 'healthy' packaged food and wonder why the weight stays.

basis.design: randomised crossover trial: each person ate both diets for 8 weeks, in random order
basis.who: UK hospital staff with overweight or obesity who usually got at least half their calories from ultra-processed food; average age 43
basis.n: 50 adults analysed (55 started; 5 of the 55 were men)
basis.measured: Weight change after 8 weeks on each diet. All food was delivered free, and both diets followed the UK's healthy-eating guide. Craving control rose 23.8 points on real food vs 12.1 on packaged food.

stats.caveat: Mostly women, and food was delivered free. Weight loss was smaller in the second diet period. 2% of body weight here was about 1.8 kg.

ref.cite: Dicken SJ, Jassil FC, Brown A, et al. (2025). Ultraprocessed or minimally processed diets following healthy dietary guidelines on weight and cardiometabolic health: a randomized, crossover trial. Nature Medicine. doi:10.1038/s41591-025-03842-0.
ref.quote: MPF (%WC, −2.06 (95% confidence interval (CI), −2.99, −1.13) and UPF (%WC, −1.05 (95% CI, −1.98, −0.13)) resulted in weight loss

stats.line: Four years after group therapy for binge eating, about 64% were fully free of binges.
stats.mirror: You want proof that beating binges lasts for years.

basis.design: 4-year follow-up of a randomised trial
basis.who: adults with binge-eating disorder and overweight, about 80% women
basis.n: 90 people (58 came back for the 4-year check)
basis.measured: No binges in the past month, about 4 years after 20 weekly group sessions: CBT 52.0%, interpersonal therapy 76.7%.

stats.caveat: One trial, mostly women; about a third did not come back at 4 years. Weight stayed about the same.

ref.cite: Hilbert A, Bishop ME, Stein RI, et al. (2012). Long-term efficacy of psychological treatments for binge eating disorder. British Journal of Psychiatry 200(3):232-237.
ref.quote: with full recovery from binge eating in 64.4% of patients

stats.line: Of US adults who had ever been overweight, about 1 in 6 had lost at least a tenth of their weight and kept it off for a year or more. For men it was 15.6%.
stats.mirror: You've lost weight before and think nobody keeps it off.

basis.design: national health survey (NHANES), one interview per person
basis.who: US adults aged 20 to 84 who had ever been overweight; 52% men
basis.measured: Highest-ever weight, weight a year ago and weight now, all as people reported them. Counted: at least 10% below the highest weight, both now and a year ago.

stats.caveat: About weight, not binges or junk food. Some of the loss may not have been on purpose, such as from illness. Weights were remembered, and one year off is not forever. Women did a little better than men (19.2% vs 15.6%).

ref.cite: Kraschnewski JL, Boan J, Esposito J, Sherwood NE, Lehman EB, Kephart DK, Sciamanna CN (2010). Long-term weight loss maintenance in the United States. International Journal of Obesity 34:1644-1654.
ref.quote: Among US adults who had ever been overweight or obese, 36.6, 17.3, 8.5 and 4.4% reported LTWLM of at least 5, 10, 15 and 20%, respectively.

stats.line: Of 784 people who lost a lot of weight and kept it off for years, a little over half used a program. The rest did it on their own.
stats.mirror: You think you need a program or a coach to change.

basis.design: survey of a registry that successful people chose to join (National Weight Control Registry)
basis.who: adults who lost an average of 30 kg and kept at least 13.6 kg off for 5 years; 155 men, 629 women
basis.measured: How they lost the weight (a formal program or on their own), what they eat and how active they are, all self-reported.

stats.caveat: About weight, not binges or junk food. Only success stories who signed up, mostly women, so it can't say which way fails more often. Both groups changed food and exercise, and 3 in 4 said a trigger event came first.

ref.cite: Klem ML, Wing RR, McGuire MT, Seagle HM, Hill JO (1997). A descriptive study of individuals successful at long-term maintenance of substantial weight loss. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition 66:239-246.
ref.quote: A little over one-half of the sample lost weight through formal programs; the remainder lost weight on their own.

stats.line: People who had already kept off 13.6 kg or more for a year still had, on average, 23 of their 31 kg off ten years later.
stats.mirror: You've lost it before and wonder if you can ever relax.

basis.design: 10-year follow-up of a registry that successful people chose to join (National Weight Control Registry)
basis.who: adults who had lost at least 13.6 kg and kept it off for at least a year; 78% women, average age 48
basis.measured: Self-reported weight each year for 10 years, plus exercise, eating habits and how often they weighed themselves.

stats.caveat: About weight, not binges or junk food. Only people already doing well when they joined, and weights were self-reported. Those who moved less, ate more freely or stopped weighing themselves regained more. The study estimates 87% were still at least 10% lighter.

ref.cite: Thomas JG, Bond DS, Phelan S, Hill JO, Wing RR (2014). Weight-loss maintenance for 10 years in the National Weight Control Registry. American Journal of Preventive Medicine 46:17-23.
ref.quote: Mean weight loss was 31.3 kg (95% CI=30.8, 31.9) at baseline, 23.8 kg (95% CI=23.2, 24.4) at 5 years and 23.1±0.4 kg (95% CI=22.3, 23.9) at 10 years.

stats.line: Fast dieters (12 weeks) and slow dieters (36 weeks) who reached their goal regained the same share of the lost weight within three years: 76%, counting dropouts. More of the fast group reached it: 81% vs 50%.
stats.mirror: You want to go all in, but everyone says go slow.

basis.design: randomised trial (fast vs slow weight loss, then a 3-year keep-it-off phase)
basis.who: adults with obesity aged 18 to 70; 51 men, 153 women enrolled
basis.n: 200 started; 127 who reached their goal began the 3-year keep-it-off phase (76 fast, 51 slow); 104 finished it
basis.measured: Share of lost weight regained 144 weeks after the weight-loss phase: 76% in both groups counting dropouts, 71% and 70.5% among those who finished. Also how many lost at least 12.5% in the time given.

stats.caveat: Most people regained most of their weight either way. This is about the pace of a diet, not about dropping junk food. Mostly women, and only those who hit their goal went on.

ref.cite: Purcell K, Sumithran P, Prendergast LA, Bouniu CJ, Delbridge E, Proietto J (2014). The effect of rate of weight loss on long-term weight management: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology 2:954-962.
ref.quote: Intention-to-treat analysis showed similar results (gradual weight loss 76·3% regain, 95% CI 65·2–87·4 vs rapid weight loss 76·3%, 65·8–86·8).

stats.line: Of US adults trying to lose weight, about 63% ate less and 63% exercised; about 42% ate less junk food or fast food.
stats.mirror: You've cut portions but kept the junk food.

basis.design: national health survey (NHANES), official statistics brief
basis.who: US adults aged 20 and over who tried to lose weight in the past 12 months; 42% of men had tried
basis.n: a national sample; the report doesn't say how many people
basis.measured: Every way people said they used to lose weight; most named two or more.

stats.caveat: Shows what people try, not what works. The ways are not split by men and women.

ref.cite: Martin CB, Herrick KA, Sarafrazi N, Ogden CL (2018). Attempts to lose weight among adults in the United States, 2013-2016. NCHS Data Brief No. 313. National Center for Health Statistics.
ref.quote: drinking a lot of water (44.7%); and eating less junk food or fast food (42.4%).

stats.line: Over two years of dieting, people who ate their craved foods less often came to crave them less. Overall, eating smaller amounts of them did not cut cravings.
stats.mirror: You've tried eating smaller bits of sweets and still crave them.

basis.design: analysis of a 2-year randomised diet trial (POUNDS Lost)
basis.who: adults with overweight or obesity on one of four calorie-cut diets; 44% men
basis.n: 367 adults at the start; 330 at 6 months and 164 at 2 years
basis.when: published 2017; checked at the start, 6 months and 2 years
basis.measured: A craving questionnaire, and how often and how much of those foods people ate, from food records.

stats.caveat: A link, not proof, and a small one. For sweets alone, eating smaller amounts also went with less craving, so cutting down is not useless.

ref.cite: Apolzan JW, Myers CA, Champagne CM, Beyl RA, Raynor HA, Anton SA, Williamson DA, Sacks FM, Bray GA, Martin CK (2017). Frequency of consuming foods predicts changes in cravings for those foods during weight loss: the POUNDS Lost Study. Obesity 25:1343-1348.
ref.quote: Altering frequency of consuming craved foods is positively associated with cravings; however, changing the amount of foods consumed does not appear to alter cravings.

stats.line: Men who did a 12-week weight program at their football club were about 5 kg lighter a year later than men on the waiting list.
stats.mirror: You think diet programs are for women, not for men like you.

basis.design: randomised trial (12 weekly group sessions at the club vs a waiting list)
basis.who: male football fans aged 35 to 65 with overweight (BMI 28 or more)
basis.measured: Weight 12 months after starting, measured by staff who did not know each man's group.

stats.caveat: About weight, not binges or junk food, in men who chose to sign up. 3.5 years on, the men still followed up were 2.9 kg lighter than at the start and about 1 in 3 weighed 5% less; the waiting-list men, who did the program a year later, did about as well.

ref.cite: Hunt K, Wyke S, Gray CM, Anderson AS, Brady A, Bunn C, Donnan PT, Fenwick E, Grieve E, Leishman J, Miller E, Mutrie N, Rauchhaus P, White A, Treweek S (2014). A gender-sensitised weight loss and healthy living programme for overweight and obese men delivered by Scottish Premier League football clubs (FFIT): a pragmatic randomised controlled trial. Lancet 383:1211-1221.
ref.quote: At 12 months the mean difference in weight loss between groups, adjusted for baseline weight and club, was 4·94 kg (95% CI 3·95-5·94)

stats.line: Teens who got water and diet drinks delivered home for a year nearly stopped sugary drinks and gained 1.9 kg less. A year after the help stopped, the gap had faded.
stats.mirror: You drink soda every day and wonder if cutting it would matter.

basis.design: randomised trial (1 year of help, then 1 year without)
basis.who: high-school students in grades 9 and 10 with overweight who drank sugary drinks or juice daily; 124 boys, 100 girls
basis.measured: Weight and BMI at 1 and 2 years; sugary drinks fell from 1.7 servings a day to nearly none. Help was home deliveries every 2 weeks, plus phone calls with parents.

stats.caveat: Teens, not grown men, and the drinks were self-reported. At 2 years, the main test, the difference was too small to be sure of, except among Hispanic teens.

ref.cite: Ebbeling CB, Feldman HA, Chomitz VR, Antonelli TA, Gortmaker SL, Osganian SK, Ludwig DS (2012). A randomized trial of sugar-sweetened beverages and adolescent body weight. New England Journal of Medicine 367:1407-1416.
ref.quote: At 1 year, however, there were significant between-group differences for changes in BMI (-0.57, P=0.045) and weight (-1.9 kg, P=0.04).

stats.line: Six months of eating less sweet food did not change how much people liked sweet taste, what they chose, or their weight. Afterwards they drifted back to their old sweet intake.
stats.mirror: You hope your sweet tooth fades if you cut sugar long enough.

basis.design: randomised trial, three groups (low, regular or high sweet diet)
basis.who: healthy adults, mostly normal weight, average age 35; 57 men, 123 women
basis.measured: Liking and sweetness of sweet foods and drinks, food choice, calories and weight, at the start, 6 months and 4 months later. About half of each day's food was supplied.

stats.caveat: Healthy volunteers, mostly women; fruit and sweeteners counted as sweet. The low group cut sweet food only from about a fifth to a seventh of its calories. A smaller earlier trial (13 people, 3 months low sugar) found pudding tasted about 40% sweeter, but was not liked any less.

ref.cite: Čad EM, Mars M, Pretorius L, van der Kruijssen M, Tang CS, de Jong HB, Balvers M, Appleton KM, de Graaf K (2026). The Sweet Tooth Trial: a parallel randomized controlled trial investigating the effects of a 6-month low, regular, or high dietary sweet taste exposure on sweet taste liking, and various outcomes related to food intake and weight status. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition 123:101073.
ref.quote: In the current trial, altering exposure to sweet-tasting foods did not change sweet taste liking, nor other outcomes.

stats.line: In therapy for binge eating, mostly CBT, about 45% of everyone who started stopped bingeing completely; 42% were still binge-free at follow-up.
stats.mirror: You think nothing will ever stop the binges.

basis.design: meta-analysis of 39 randomised trials
basis.who: adults with binge-eating disorder; 65 treatment groups, 40 of them CBT
basis.measured: Share with zero binges at the end of treatment: 45.1% of all who started, 50.9% of those who finished. At follow-up: 42.3% and 50.3%.

stats.caveat: Zero binges is a strict bar; many others improve partly. Interpersonal therapy had the highest rates.

ref.cite: Linardon J (2018). Rates of abstinence following psychological or behavioral treatments for binge-eating disorder: meta-analysis. International Journal of Eating Disorders 51(8):785-797.
ref.quote: The total weighted percentage of patients who achieved abstinence at posttreatment in the intention-to-treat analysis (all randomized patients) was 45.1% (95% CI =40.7, 49.5)

rejected.claim: Regular meals (no skipping) reduce binge eating, with a number
rejected.why: No fetched study gave a number for regular eating on its own; it is one part of CBT. Not used.
Abstract gives no effect size; girls only. Already in the page's whatWorks; no new number.

rejected.claim: Fat plus carbohydrate foods are valued more than either alone (DiFeliceantonio 2018)
rejected.why: Abstract has no sample size or number. Not used.

rejected.claim: Hilbert 2019 meta-analysis (81 trials, 7,515 people): CBT remission rate
rejected.why: Abstract gives effect sizes, not a remission percentage; used Linardon 2018 abstinence rates instead.

rejected.claim: Ultra-processed food raises depression odds 1.55x (Menon 2026, NHANES 2021-23)
rejected.why: Measured ultra-processed food only by added sugar; weak method. Not used.

rejected.claim: Lane 2024 umbrella review: deaths from heart disease and all causes
rejected.why: Death counts left out on the owner's rule; only anxiety and sleep used.

rejected.claim: Praxedes 2022: food addiction 20% overall, 55% in people with binge eating
rejected.why: Checks out (PMID 34953001, fetched). Named in the hero caveat as the higher pooled figure; the hero leads with the lower 14%.

rejected.claim: Hero line '14% of adults meet the threshold for food addiction'
rejected.why: Matches the BMJ text. Kept 14% as the conservative figure; the hero caveat now says another pooling with clinic patients found 20%.

rejected.claim: Ultra-processed food raises the odds of anxiety (1.48) and sleep problems (1.41) (Lane 2024 umbrella review)
rejected.why: Fetched the source meta-analyses: the anxiety figure pools 3 snapshot studies (101,709 people), 100,648 of them from one survey of Brazilian teenagers (Lane 2022, PMC9268228). The sleep meta-analysis (Delpino 2023, 15 cross-sectional studies) found no crude link in adults. Too weak, and not about young men.

rejected.claim: Over five years, most young women with binge-eating disorder recovered; 18% (7 of 40) still had an eating disorder (Fairburn 2000, Oxford)
rejected.why: Women only (48 at the start, 40 at 5 years), so a male reader cannot honestly see himself in it. The 4-year trial result (64% binge-free) covers recovery instead.

rejected.claim: About 4 in 100 US men have had any binge eating, milder cases included (Hudson 2007)
rejected.why: Checks out (full text, 1,220 men); folded into the 2.0% stat's basis so the same men are not shown twice.

rejected.claim: US men aged 20 to 39 get 249 kcal and 9.3% of their daily calories from sugary drinks (NCHS Data Brief 270, 2011-2014)
rejected.why: Fetched brief and data tables: neither gives how many men aged 20 to 39 were surveyed, so the number behind the figure is unknown. Left out; a good sugar stat if a source with the sample size turns up.

rejected.claim: Swapping sugary drinks for water or diet drinks for 6 months gave 2 to 2.5% weight loss (Tate 2012, CHOICE trial, 318 adults).
rejected.why: PMID 22301929, abstract checked: 84% women, and weight loss did not differ from a control group making changes of their choosing. Used the Ebbeling 2012 trial (224 teens, about half boys) for sugary drinks instead.

rejected.claim: Smaller portions and packages could cut 144 to 228 kcal a day (Hollands 2015 Cochrane review, 72 studies).
rejected.why: PMID 26368271, abstract checked: mostly single-meal lab studies at unclear or high risk of bias; the daily kcal figure is the authors' projection if smaller sizes were kept across the whole diet. Too indirect for a number on the page.

rejected.claim: Obese adults who ate less fat, exercised more, used prescription drugs or joined commercial programs were likelier to lose 5 to 10% (Nicklas 2012, NHANES, 2,523 who tried).
rejected.why: PMID 22516488, abstract checked: one-time survey of self-reported strategies, so the links may run either way; overlaps the NCHS 2018 'ways people try' stat.

rejected.claim: After 3 months on a low-sugar diet, sweet food tastes about 40% sweeter (Wise 2016).
rejected.why: PMID 26607941, abstract checked: only 13 people finished the low-sugar arm, and liking did not change. Kept as a caveat on the larger Sweet Tooth trial.

rejected.claim: Five years after a structured weight-loss program, the average person keeps off about 3 kg (Anderson 2001 meta-analysis, 29 US studies).
rejected.why: PMID 11684524, abstract checked: older programs (many very-low-calorie diets) and no head count in the summary. The Purcell 2014 trial shows regain more directly.
Not checked this round. A drug trial number would read like an advert on a habits page, and the brief asked for method shares only.
